This pretraining paradigm has interesting implications for both the future of language models, and potentially how we think about human Universal Grammar.

paper.title: From Puzzle-Solver to Language Model: Recurrent Inductive Bias, Data Scale, and Benchmark Validity in BabyLM
paper.abstract: In the small-data regime of the BabyLM Challenge, a model’s architecture still shapes what it learns. We ask how much an inductive bias toward recurrence helps, and whether current benchmarks can detect that help. Our model adapts the Hierarchical Reasoning Model, a small recurrent puzzle-solver that reuses one shared block many times per token instead of stacking more layers. We make three changes to turn it into a language model: a sequence-mixing layer that can carry order-dependent state, a gate on one of the two connections between its modules, and a tunable number of recurrent cycles. The result matches a parameter-matched GPT-2, and we use it to study three questions. Q1: recurrence buys depth without adding parameters. On a controlled state-tracking task, running more cycles of the same weights tracks longer sequences, even when the extra cycles are added only at inference. Q2: the advantage is largest where data is scarcest. leads GPT-2 on BLiMP at words, ties at , and, trained to convergence, still leads at tokens (out of budget, where data and tokenizer also change). Q3: the benchmark meant to reward state-tracking cannot see it. A null model that never reads the puzzle outscores every trained model on entity_tracking, because 28.5% of its items reveal the answer in the option list and every trained model is at chance on the rest. Gains on that task measure how well a model has learned the frequency of one answer. Because the suite misses a capability we can demonstrate directly, we recommend pairing benchmarks with controlled architectural probes.

paper.title: Language Allocation and Targeted Data Design for a Multilingual BabyLM
paper.abstract: Under a fixed multilingual pretraining budget, we study how language allocation, data design, and model configuration affect English–Dutch–Chinese pretraining. First, we trained three fixed language mixtures with three matched seeds. No pairwise difference in the mean of seven zero-shot benchmarks used for model selection was significant after Holm correction. Language-specific scores nevertheless differed: the 50/25/25 mixture scored 2.487 points higher than 27.5/27.5/45 in English, whereas 27.5/27.5/45 scored 2.151 points higher than 40/40/20 in Chinese, after correction within each language. In a 25M-word proxy experiment, an inverse-score controller changed language exposure but did not improve the aggregate score. Second, across four matched seeds, the targeted-augmentation condition scored higher on ZS16 than the real-text baseline (57.37 versus 56.57). The largest language-specific difference was observed for Chinese (+1.47). Both the ZS16 and Chinese differences remained significant after Holm correction over the four reported tests. Across three matched seeds, multi-token prediction showed no detectable improvement in ZS16. In single-run comparisons across parameter counts, the 213M-parameter model had the highest observed FT22 score (41.25). We treat all parameter-count comparisons and the remaining tokenizer and data ablations as descriptive because each used a single run. The 213M-parameter model obtained a leaderboard-reported Multilingual Average of 50.68.

paper.title: Feeding BabyLMs Macaroni: Code-Switching Curricula Cause Cross-Lingual Convergence

paper.abstract: Children in multilingual communities often code-switch, using multiple languages in a single utterance. Can we induce cross-lingual alignment in language models by training on code-switched text? We pretrain small decoder-only transformers on two 100M-word multilingual corpora: a base corpus formed by mixing the English, Dutch, and Chinese BabyBabelLM datasets, and a corpus generated from it by inserting word- and sentence-level code-switching using an LLM. We find that training on code-switched data aligns the representations of parallel text, particularly across different scripts, and that this alignment persists through training on monolingual documents. Under a learning curriculum that progresses from word-level code-switching, to sentence-level code-switching, to monolingual documents, models trained on code-switched data outperform baselines trained without it on the BabyLM evaluation suite. Our work characterizes code-switching curriculum learning as an effective data augmentation method for multilingual pretraining. We release our code, data, and models at https://github.com/drooryck/multilingual-macaroni.

paper.title: Parameter-Efficient Architectures for Developmentally Plausible Pretraining: Optimizing Embedding and Projection Layers under BabyLM Strict-Small Constraints
paper.abstract: The BabyLM Strict-Small track asks whether language models can acquire robust linguistic generalizations from only 10 million words, a regime in which standard scaling practices leave little room for architectural waste. We study one such source of waste: the dense vocabulary-by-hidden-size embedding and output projection layers used by conventional Transformer encoders.Under a BabyLM-sized corpus, these layers devote millions of trainable parameters to a Zipfian long tail of subword types that receive sparse and noisy updates. Using a compact ModernBERT-style encoder as our baseline, we conduct a controlled comparison of 15 embedding configurations, including ALBERT-style factorization, nonlinear factorized projections, tensor-train embeddings, deterministic Fourier features over token identities, and byte-ngram composition with token residuals, frequency gating, and geometry regularization. We identify tied linear factorization and byte-ngram composition as the strongest parameter-quality tradeoffs in this comparison.

paper.title: XpertGPT: Multi-Scale Sparse Expert Routing for Data-Constrained Language Modeling
paper.abstract: We introduce XpertGPT, a sparse decoder-only Transformer for data-constrained language modelling that routes tokens to parallel expert pathways operating at multiple contextual scales. Under the BabyLM strict-small budget of roughly ten million words, conventional dense Transformers spend identical computation on every token and impose a single fixed receptive field. Each XpertGPT layer pairs a dense global-attention stream with four sparse sliding-window expert branches, whose attention spans range from 64 down to 4 tokens, chosen by Expert-Choice routing that balances expert load by construction without any auxiliary loss, and applies rotary position embeddings and gated feed-forward networks throughout. Trained on the BabyLM 2026 Strict-Small corpus, our 52.6M-parameter model reaches an overall average of 38.42, surpassing the official GPT-2(98.4M) baseline (37.38) across grammatical acceptability, world-knowledge, and language-understanding benchmarks.

paper.title: BabyConceptLM: Exploring Dynamic Concept Computation under Restricted Language Exposure
paper.abstract: Human language learning takes place under limited exposure and is shaped by structured regularities in the input, whereas standard Transformers apply a largely uniform sequence of computations at every token position. We ask whether dynamic latent segmentation can provide a useful inductive bias for language modeling under BabyLM-scale data constraints. BabyConceptLM causally encodes tokens, groups contextual states into learned contiguous latent segments, processes the shorter sequence with a deeper latent-level backbone, and returns to token resolution through a leakage-safe causal readout. We evaluate two profiles using recipe-matched token-only controls, with analyses of computational cost and segmentation behavior. Across English, multilingual, and Chinese comparisons, BabyConceptLM trails matched token-only controls by 0.60–1.47 points. Estimated padding-aware dense-forward FLOPs are reduced by 26% and 39% for the English and multilingual 5/8/3 models, respectively, but increase for the Chinese 2/4/2 configuration. Segmentation audits show weak alignment with word boundaries and predominantly length-driven behavior, with the larger model frequently reaching its eight-token segment cap. These results show that latent segmentation can yield a favorable compute–accuracy trade-off in some configurations, but does not by itself produce linguistically structured units or improved predictive performance. BabyConceptLM serves as a diagnostic test of hierarchical latent computation under restricted language exposure.

paper.title: Introducing Code-Switched Contexts to Cognitively-Inspired Bilingual Model Training
paper.abstract: During language acquisition, bilingual children are regularly exposed to code-switched input and use it as a cognitive scaffold to accelerate vocabulary growth and cross-linguistic syntactic mapping. In contrast, computational bilingual models are conventionally pretrained on interleaved monolingual corpora. While introducing synthetic code-switching during pretraining has become a promising strategy to enhance cross-lingual alignment and downstream performance, the structural and developmental parameters governing the success remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate the efficiency of training with synthetic code-switched data across two typologically distinct language pairs by controlling two key variables: the structural location of code-switches and the dynamic switching rate across training stages. Our results show that training with code-switched data improves cross-lingual alignment for typologically close languages.

paper.title: BabySteps at BabyLM 2026: Stronger Optimization and Causal Baselines for Data-Constrained Pretraining
paper.abstract: We present three BabySteps systems that strengthen baselines for data-constrained pretraining in the strict-small (10M words) and strict (100M words) NLP tracks of the 2026 BabyLM Challenge. Across our GPT-BERT experiments, optimizer choice and learning-rate tuning produced our largest gains, highlighting the importance of well-tuned baselines for evaluating progress in sample-efficient pretraining. The curriculum, synthetic-data, teacher-supervision, and corpus-mixing interventions that we tested did not improve the final aggregate score.We also test whether the official GPT-2 checkpoint is a sufficiently strong reference for causal language modeling. A 127.6M-parameter Llama-style decoder trained with Muon and Liger-optimized kernels obtains a seven-suite NLP average of 56.18, compared with 52.79 for our completed reevaluation of the official BabyLM GPT-2 strict checkpoint, and scores higher on all seven categories. This is not a controlled architectural ablation: architecture, optimizer, implementation, and hyperparameters change together. Instead, it provides a stronger practical causal baseline. In addition, we report failed data interventions, a numerical failure caused by batches with no supervised target tokens, and substantial variance between small evaluation suites.

paper.title: Learning What Can Combine and What Can Substitute: Relational Inductive Biases for BabyLM Pretraining
paper.abstract: Language can produce many expressions from a limited set of units because linguistic units participate in two basic relations. Syntagmatic relations determine which units can combine, while paradigmatic relations determine which units can substitute for one another in the same position. We study whether explicitly learning these relations helps language models generalize from limited data. We introduce two auxiliary objectives for masked language modeling. The Syntagmatic objective aligns a masked representation with relevant context selected by attention, while the Paradigmatic objective aligns it with the embedding neighbors of the target token. Both objectives are generated by the model itself and require no additional data, annotation, or trainable parameters. Experiments on BabyLM 2026 Strict-Small show that both single-relation systems improve mean Overall performance over Standard MLM, with Paradigmatic giving the most consistent gains across three seeds. Relay Joint combines the two objectives and shows a strong neighborhood-alignment signal at its submitted checkpoint, although its downstream gains vary across seeds. These results suggest that relational objectives can provide useful learning signals under limited data, while stronger internal alignment does not always lead to more stable downstream performance. Code is now publicly available on GitHub.

paper.title: Domain-Based Routing in Mixture-of-Experts Models for BabyLMs
paper.abstract: Recent language model improvements were mostly achieved by increasing model scale, compute, and in particular training data size. This differs significantly from human language acquisition, which relies on significantly fewer words. The BabyLM challenge tackles this issue by encouraging approaches inspired by cognitive insights to reduce data dependency, thus lowering the barrier for NLP researchers to contribute to their field. We propose a Mixture-of-Experts approach with guided domain-based routing to learn subnetworks specialized on human-interpretable topics, thus making experts focus on domain knowledge and style rather than specific token features. Additionally, we apply a CEFR-based curriculum learning to mimic human language learning. Our model underperforms compared to the 7 times larger baseline model, but scores best on the BabyLM strict-small leaderboard among models with less than 25M parameters. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/SmallLM-DBR-MoE-Submission-2026/Baby-DBR, and our model can be found at https://huggingface.co/elschr/BabyLM2026-DBR.

paper.title: Dense Supervision, Gentle Decay: Curriculum-Guided Rebalancing of ELECTRA-Style RTD and MLM for Small-Data Pretraining
paper.abstract: When training data is very limited, the way different training signals are weighted over time can strongly affect what a model learns. We study hybrid replaced-token detection (RTD) and masked language modeling (MLM) pretraining under the BabyLM 2026 Strict-Small budget. We train five single-seed DeBERTa-v2 models along three curriculum axes: objective scheduling, masking policy, and data order. The primary system, bgb-decay, retains generator MLM, discriminator RTD, and auxiliary discriminator MLM throughout training while reducing the RTD coefficient in stages. We compare it with a matched fixed-RTD reference, a variant that adds easy-to-hard data ordering and adaptive auxiliary masking, and two stronger RTD-to-MLM handoff schedules with whole-word and adaptive masking. Among the five runs, bgb-decay achieves the best overall balance, while the more aggressive variants gain more on some tasks but drop more on others. Training diagnostics reveal a trade-off between replacement discrimination and auxiliary vocabulary prediction: under fixed high RTD weighting, RTD gradients are larger and nearly orthogonal to auxiliary-MLM gradients, while staged decay preserves RTD but shifts late optimization toward MLM. These results suggest that gradual objective rebalancing is a promising direction for small-data pretraining.

paper.title: Tokens of Meaning: Semantically-Informed Morphological Tokenization in Low-Resource Language Modeling
paper.abstract: Subword tokenizers for language models are typically trained to efficiently encode text into short sequences of reusable units. These often produce tokens which are not linguistically meaningful, such as giraffe –> g ira ffe. We ask whether a tokenizer that instead splits words into semantically meaningful morphemes can help a language model learn under a developmentally plausible data budget, where every training token is scarce and sharing evidence across related word forms should matter most. We build such a tokenizer for English by hand-curating a word-to-morpheme-segmentation dictionary, built on top of MorphyNet, a database of derivational and inflectional morphology. Each word is only split into morphemes when the pieces are productive and the whole word’s meaning is semantically related to them, thus splitting unhappiness into un happy ness, but keeping business whole. On the 10M-word BabyLM corpus this holds out-of-vocabulary tokens to 1.0%, with an inventory of ~37k tokens. We compare the tokenizer intrinsically against both statistical (BPE, Unigram, WordPiece) and morphology-aware (Morfessor, MorphPiece) baselines, and measure its effect on a child-scale language model. In a controlled comparison against an uncurated baseline built from the same morphological source, curation yields +1.4 BLiMP. Our submitted model, which adds masked next-token prediction and vocabulary pruning, reaches 72.53 BLiMP and ranks second on COMPS and third on EWoK on the BabyLM 2026 strict-small leaderboard.

paper.title: What Does Input-Dependent Depth Routing Buy in Data-Limited Language Modeling?
paper.abstract: Learned weighting of earlier layers, as used in ELC-BERT (Charpentier and Samuel, 2023), is a promising direction for sample-efficient language modeling. Attention Residuals (AttnRes; Kimi Team et al., 2026) extend this idea by computing input-dependent weights separately for each token, with reported gains in large-scale autoregressive models. We present a controlled study of whether such input-dependent depth routing helps in the data-limited regime where static routing first proved useful. Across the 10M- and 100M-word BabyLM budgets and three paired seeds, AttnRes consistently lowers test negative log-likelihood (NLL) compared to a residual baseline. It reaches the same development-set (dev) NLL after seeing fewer training words. In the 10M L32 control, AttnRes also lowers test NLL relative to static routing in all three seeds. Behavioral differences between AttnRes and the baseline are small and mixed. The BLiMP (Warstadt et al., 2020) advantage at equal training exposure disappears after matching on dev NLL. The trained 10M-word AttnRes models make causal use of routes from nonrecent depth blocks, but we find no clear evidence that categories with greater dependence on these sources achieve larger BLiMP gains over the baseline.

paper.title: Language Exposure Matters: Distribution and Order in Multilingual BabyLM Pre-training
paper.abstract: We investigate the effects of multilingual pre-training with limited data by addressing the problem of how language exposure should be distributed and ordered across English, Dutch, and Chinese. In particular, we compare balanced multilingual exposure to language-dominant exposure, where one language is exposed with more training data than the others. We also compare mixed training, where multilingual training data is used throughout training, with curriculum training, where monolingual exposure of the dominant language is followed by balanced multilingual exposure. Our results show that multilingual BabyLM performance varies with both the amount and order of language exposure. Mixed training outperforms curriculum learning across all 15 matched configurations, indicating that simultaneous multilingual exposure is more effective than staged exposure in our setting. For each primary language, the best language-dominant mixed training configuration outperforms the balanced configuration, suggesting that an equal distribution is not necessarily optimal under a limited data budget. Interestingly, the Dutch-primary configurations achieve the best overall performance.

paper.title: Looped GPT-BERT: Trading Parameters for Computation in Small Language Modeling
paper.abstract: When training data are limited, increasing parameter count is not the only way to improve language-model performance. A small parameter set, when repeatedly applied, can also deliver comparable performance. We study Looped GPT-BERT in the BabyLM 2026 Strict-small setting, combining GPT-BERT’s masked next-token and causal language-modeling objectives with depth-wise parameter sharing. We train on a preprocessed 7.48M-word English corpus and compare objective ratios, non-looped and looped architectures, and loop counts. Our final 4\times12 model uses four physical layers for twelve recurrent traversals and contains 12.18M parameters. The BabyLM 2026 leaderboard reports an Overall Average of 35.42 and an NLP Average of 48.48. Compared with public BabyLM 10M Strict-small GPT-2 and GPT-BERT baselines, it achieves comparable performance on selected linguistic and downstream metrics, including BLiMP and GLUE, with fewer parameters. The loop ablations show that additional recurrent computation can improve training and preserve strong performance on selected linguistic tasks, whereas poorer performance on other tasks may reveal an inherent limitation of the looped design: using only a few physical layers restricts the model’s representational space.
